In physics, it is useful to organize the description of a physical situation around the following triad: (System, State of the System, Propositions about the System).

The System is simply the physical system under study. The State of the System is a mathematical entity that encodes the information provided by the physical theory about the system (usually at a given time, so the state of the system evolves in time). The Propositions about the System are statements one can make about the system (for example, if the system is a localizable particle, a valid proposition is $P=$ “the position of the particle is $x=5\,\mathrm{cm}$”). There is a key relation between the state of the system and these propositions that allows the theory to make predictions. The propositions do not have, a priori, any assigned truth value (i.e., true or false). If the system is in a state $S$, and this state encodes all the information supplied by the theory, one can ask: when the system is in that state, what is the truth value of proposition $P$? Or at least, what is the probability that proposition $P$ is true? We denote this probability by $S(P)$. In this sense, given a state $S$, one can take all propositions $P$ about the system and ask what is the probability that $P$ is true when the state is $S$. Physically, the probability can be interpreted in the usual frequency sense: if one performs many similar experiments measuring the truth value of the proposition, the fraction of experiments in which it is true approaches the corresponding probability. The quantity $S(P)$ is the value predicted by the theory in this large-sample limit.

The structure becomes more interesting at this point. In classical physics, the standard models imply that the set of all propositions $P$ about the system has a well-known structure (called the “logic of the system”): a Boolean algebra. A property that characterizes this is distributivity, i.e., for any propositions $P$, $Q$, and $R$, and if “and” and “or” are the usual logic operators, then we always have

$$
P\wedge(Q\vee R)=(P\wedge Q)\vee(P\wedge R).
$$

Using the structure of the models, the notation $S(P)$ can be taken quite literally: the state $S$ can be viewed as a function from the set of all possible propositions to the subset $[0,1]$ of real numbers. Thus, $S$ acts on a proposition $P$ and returns a number $S(P)$, the probability that this proposition is true in this state (mathematically, the set of propositions is the Borel sigma-algebra of phase space and $S$ is a measure in this set). A key property is that this structure allows what are called “sharp states” or “deterministic states”. These states can take only the values $1$ and $0$. Thus, for any proposition $P$, $S(P)$ is either $1$ or $0$: the proposition is predicted to be true or false with certainty. The important point is that, given such a state, the truth value of any proposition about the system can be predicted with certainty. These states therefore provide a deterministic description. There are also states that are not of this type; these are probabilistic states. Since the theory allows deterministic states, probabilities need not be interpreted as reflecting a fundamental stochasticity of the system; they may instead reflect insufficiently precise knowledge of the initial conditions. In this sense, the underlying classical system is regarded as deterministic because such sharp states exist.

Now consider the quantum case. The classical picture above has a fundamental problem: it conflicts with experiment. The structure of the set of all possible propositions, the logic of the system, is more complicated. For example, there are propositions that are called “incompatible”: if $P$ and $Q$ are incompatible, it is not meaningful to ask about the truth value of the proposition $P\wedge Q$ since the logical operator “and” is not defined in this case (for example, in the double-slit experiment, if $P=$ “an interference pattern will be observed on the screen” and $Q=$ “the electron went through slit 1” are incompatible, since the measurement of the truth value of one affects the truth value of the other; as observed experimentally, the measurement of the truth value of $Q$ destroys the interference pattern). The assumptions in the triad must therefore be relaxed (System, State of the System, Propositions about the System): now, the logic of the system is something more general than the classical Boolean algebra. The question is then what mathematical structure can accommodate incompatible propositions. The classical Borel sigma-algebra cannot do so, because it is Boolean. The answer was first developed by John von Neumann. I will not go into the mathematical details here. The essential point is that the set of all possible propositions can be seen as the set of orthogonal projectors in a Hilbert space. This gives a new mathematical formalism for the triad that accommodates incompatible propositions. This formalism is what we call quantum mechanics. The resulting theory has properties that differ substantially from the classical formalism. Consider now its possible states. A state $S$ is again a function from the set of all possible propositions to the subset $[0,1]$ of real numbers, but now the set of propositions is the set of orthogonal projectors in a Hilbert space. Gleason's theorem completely characterizes the states available in this formalism. A central consequence is that sharp states of the classical kind are not allowed; the states are probabilistic.

What does this mean? From the point of view of prediction, it means giving up the possibility of assigning the truth values of all propositions with complete certainty. One may still ask whether this necessarily makes the world non-deterministic. A possible answer is no: perhaps the formalism is incomplete, and additional principles, assumptions, or hidden variables could restore sharp states. A deterministic theory of this type would have to admit sharp states so that the same interpretation used in classical physics could be recovered. This is problematic within the present framework. As above, these states tend to be associated with classical logics. Adding such states would therefore conflict with a core assumption of the framework, namely that the logic is non-classical. Within this formulation, this would amount to imposing mutually incompatible assumptions on the theory. One possible way around this is to say that the quantum logic only represents statements about measurements (which necessarily involves the interaction between the measurement apparatus and the system) and the classical logic the “true” properties of the system. In this way, the non-classical features of the quantum logic arise because of the unavoidable interaction between the measurement apparatus and the system.

A common conclusion is therefore that the probabilistic character of quantum mechanics is not merely a reflection of classical ignorance, but follows from principles that differ from those of classical physics.

Alternative interpretations, such as Bohmian mechanics, avoid this conclusion by introducing additional structure and features such as contextuality. From the present point of view, this makes them less economical than the standard interpretation: they are not merely hidden-variable completions, but require further physical and interpretive assumptions.
